name: Salvia

project_scope.note: Salvia comparison set completed with ten canonical species. S. greggii and S. lyrata remain range-evidence exceptions approved by the user; their species files preserve UNRESOLVED strict-range status.

shared_traits: two fertile stamens with elongate connective/lever architecture
flowers grouped in cymes/verticils along a flowering axis
priority: salvia-texana vs salvia-engelmannii: count basal vs cauline leaves and flower cymes, study calyx glands only with macros
salvia-farinacea vs salvia-azurea: mealy calyx vs open tall flower axis and narrow leaves
salvia-coccinea vs salvia-roemeriana vs salvia-pentstemonoides: separate basal leaf patterns, habitat and flower size
salvia-greggii vs salvia-ballotiflora: woody shrubs and distinctive leaves/calyces
salvia-lyrata: deeply lyrate rosette leaf vs other blue flowered sages
calyx surface, ribs, and lobe tips
study_strategy.warning: Do not identify Texas sages primarily by flower color. Several local species overlap in blue-violet shades.

quick_key.if: broad triangular/deltoid leaves on conspicuous petioles; tall red-flowered sage
tall perennial with narrow linear leaves and long open flowering axis; calyx green and not mealy
low perennial with basal + cauline leaves, sunken/pitted glandular hairs, sharply pointed ribbed calyx
low dense clump, only cauline narrow leaves, tack-shaped glands, 3-flowered cymes
mealy/farinose calyx on an erect perennial with lanceolate cauline leaves
basal rosette in shaded Ashe-juniper habitat with red tubular flowers
woody shrub with tiny rough hairy leaves and small blue-purple flowers
large basal rosette, tall stalk, and unusually large red/rose flowers in limestone seep or canyon habitat
woody aromatic shrub with small elliptic leaves and comparatively large showy flowers
flat basal rosette of deeply lyrate leaves with a mostly leafless flowering stalk and small blue-lavender flowers

shared_genus_recognition.look_here_first: FIRST identify the growth form (shrub, annual herb, or low perennial); then whole-plant leaves, then the flowering node and calyx. Tiny leaf gland shapes are strong when correctly photographed but cannot be guessed from a fuzzy full-plant shot.
shared_traits: two fertile stamens with elongate connective/lever architecture
flowers grouped in cymes/verticils along a flowering axis
shared_genus_recognition.science_caution: S. texana has basal leaves but is not itself a true basal rosette (UT Austin); never claim basal rosette in that species. Also many blue-violet Salvia have strongly ribbed calyces: ribs alone are NOT a reliable species ID.

key_traits.texana: Basal AND cauline leaves but NOT true rosette; basal leaf 25–60 × 4–10+ mm
key_traits.engelmannii: Only cauline leaves, slender linear ~30–60 × 3–5 mm
key_traits.why: Best whole-plant difference if base in frame
key_traits.photo_requirements: Photograph full rooted base on each plant, and paired leaves on 1-mm ruler

key_traits.look: Flower groups at same stem node
key_traits.texana: Terminal many-flowered axis/raceme; often 8–14 flower pairs, sharply pointed leafy bracts
key_traits.engelmannii: Two opposing axillary cymes with three flowers per cyme, often close nodes
key_traits.why: Teaches difference between individual flower pairs and multi-flower branching cymes
key_traits.photo_requirements: Same-level flowering node side close-up with visible pedicels, no overlapping labels

key_traits.texana: Glandular hairs embedded/sunken in pits on leaf and calyx
key_traits.engelmannii: Subsessile tack-shaped glands stand above leaf/calyx surface
key_traits.why: Microstructure true separator when adequately photographed
key_traits.photo_requirements: Exact species same-magnification leaf/calyx macro, millimeter scale and arrows directly on confirmed glands; not available yet

key_traits.engelmannii: 10-ribbed calyx ~10–11 mm with ~0.5-mm awn tips and raised tack glands
key_traits.photo_requirements: Side/back photo of same-maturity calyces at ruler scale

key_traits.engelmannii: Pale blue-violet, often very white/violet-marked lower lip
key_traits.why: Flower color/brightness varies and cannot be sole split
key_traits.photo_requirements: Same light, angle, camera and stage for both species

photo_comparison_focus.memory_rule: TEXANA = basal leaves + PIT glands + pointed leafy bracts. ENGELMANN = stem leaves only + TACK glands + three-flower cymes.
do_not_label_without_macro: one flower in a 3-flowered cyme when pedicels not separately visible

field_vocabulary.basal: BAY-sul — near plant base; basal leaves do NOT always make a rosette
field_vocabulary.rosette: roh-ZET — tight cluster of leaves at ground-level crown
field_vocabulary.cyme: SIME — flowering group with branching pedicels; count separate flowers in each
field_vocabulary.raceme: ray-SEEM — mostly unbranched flower axis with individual flower stalks
field_vocabulary.verticil: VER-ti-sil — flowers grouped around one node, often opposite cymes
field_vocabulary.gland: GLAND — minute secretory structure; can sit sunken (pit) or raised (tack)
field_vocabulary.farinose: far-ih-NOSE — densely coated in short powdery-looking hairs, not actual flour
field_vocabulary.calyx: KAY-liks — green or purplish outer cup behind a flower
field_vocabulary.rib: A raised longitudinal ridge on a calyx or stem
field_vocabulary.rhizome: RY-zohm — underground horizontal stem that can make new shoots
field_vocabulary.trichome: TRY-kohm — a plant hair; its density and color can be diagnostic
field_vocabulary.foliolate: FOH-lee-uh-lit — divided into identifiable leaflets; 3-foliolate means three separate leaflet blades
field_vocabulary.petiole: PET-ee-ohl — the stalk attaching a leaf blade to a stem
field_vocabulary.peltate: PEL-tayt — stalk attached under the leaf blade, not at the edge; cedar sage can only LOOK almost peltate
field_vocabulary.corolla: kuh-ROLL-uh — all joined petals including the flower tube and lips
field_vocabulary.lyrate: LYE-rate — a leaf widest at a rounded tip lobe, with smaller side lobes nearer the petiole
field_vocabulary.lobe: Part of the SAME leaf blade bounded by notches
field_vocabulary.leaflet: A SEPARATE blade forming part of a compound leaf
field_vocabulary.crenate: KREE-nayt — margin with rounded shallow teeth
field_vocabulary.axillary: AK-sill-air-ee — arising from an angle between leaf and stem

photo_review_cautions: Some pre-existing Salvia texana photo records have unresolved photographer and rights; study-only, not public export.
One Commons photo titled 'Blue Sage / Texas Sage' (4553958082) says 'Could be Engelmann’s Salvia' on its source page; exclude from learner despite correct-looking Commons category.
UT Williamson specimen says texana NOT rosetted; distinguish basal leaves from true rosette.

Canonical Salvia texana range record counts Williamson as a target county, but Williamson is NOT within project 24-county zone. Flag to science/range lane for reconciliation, without changing a settled status in this PHOTO lane.
Farinacea has BOTH white-felted and dark-violet-felted calyx forms, UT Austin local description; 'not white' does not rule it out.
S. azurea local var. grandiflora differs in taxonomic scope from the Florida var. azurea diagnostic photo; show provenance in every panel.

Salvia azurea AND farinacea canonical PASS county lists also count Williamson, outside the target-zone list: flag for separate 3-county recertification, do not alter this science decision in visual lane.
Salvia ballotiflora UT Hays Flora introduced from Medina County — don't count as wild Hays native.
Salvia ballotiflora current strict PASS uses Val Verde outside target zone; needs scientific range recertification, separate from visual learner.
Shrubby blue two additional Commons images have unknown individual credits/licenses and must remain private-only pending audit.
Lyreleaf Texas winter rosette photographed Anderson County, outside target; photo doesn't fix unresolved nativity status.
Autumn sage cultivars/hybrids may mislead; glossy smooth leaf/large flower is supportive only.

photo_comparison_groups.name: Red-Flowered Sage Trio
photo_comparison_groups.look_here_first: Plant BASE and COMPLETE LEAF before red flowers. Scarlet: simple, stem-leafy annual; cedar: true perennial woodland rosette, sometimes 1–3 leaflets; big red: large smooth dark green rosette and big ~4 cm corollas.

comparison_matrix.coccinea: Upright leafy annual/short-lived perennial; generally branched stems, not typical thick rosette
comparison_matrix.roemeriana: Taprooted perennial, LOW leaf rosette and stem leaves
comparison_matrix.pentstemonoides: Long-lived perennial with thick smooth rosette leaves to ~12 cm, stout flowering stalk to ~1.5 m

comparison_matrix.coccinea: ONE simple broad triangular/ovate serrated blade on petiole; many stem leaves
comparison_matrix.roemeriana: Often LONG petioled, simple or 1–3 leaflets; cordate/broad terminal leaflet and optional two smaller lateral leaflets
comparison_matrix.pentstemonoides: Smooth thick dark green large basal blade; not characteristically a three-leaflet leaf

comparison_matrix.coccinea: Scarlet red two-lipped tubes on successive whorls; flowering color cultivars vary
comparison_matrix.roemeriana: Crimson tubes, with flower cymes usually 3 flowers each; calyx ~11 mm
comparison_matrix.pentstemonoides: Large reddish-purple/pink-red flowers ~4 cm long; much larger on average; calyx aging green to purple

comparison_matrix.coccinea: Variable: open/disturbed or lightly shaded beds/woodlands
comparison_matrix.roemeriana: Often juniper duff, rocky woodland shade
comparison_matrix.pentstemonoides: Seep-fed, often shaded limestone bluffs and ravines near creeks; rare endemic

comparison_matrix.coccinea: Cultivar color, red/orange intensity not absolute
comparison_matrix.roemeriana: 1-foliolate leaves can look simple; nearly-peltate petiole impression isn't peltate
comparison_matrix.pentstemonoides: Young small plants or dried rosettes may look like cedar; check flowers/scale and habitat

photo_comparison_groups.memory_rule: SCARLET = SIMPLE STEM LEAVES. CEDAR = SHADY ROSETTE, MAYBE 3 LEAFLETS. BIG RED = BIG SMOOTH ROSETTE + ~4-CM FLOWERS.
field_photo_instructions: 1. Whole rooted plant including base, 2. one mature leaf showing stalk and any side leaflets, 3. side flower with a centimeter ruler, 4. opposite cymes and individual pedicels, 5. calyx behind corolla. Compare in same photo scale.

look_here_first: For blue/purple sages: first check whole plant and opposite leaves, then a SIDE VIEW of the CALYX behind the corolla. In azurea vs farinacea, green visibly ribbed versus dense white-or-purple fuzzy calyx. In texana vs engelmannii, basal+stem leaves versus stem-only, then pit/tack glands. Avoid identifying from blue flower alone.
